questions.question: What do critics praise about Mad Max: Fury Road?
questions.answer:
Critics consistently praise the film's visual and technical craft, pacing, and performances:

- **Visuals & technical craft:** Ian Nathan (Empire Magazine, 5/5) hails "jaw-dropping action" and "barking-mad imagination"; Bruce Kirkland (Toronto Sun, 4/5) praises the "sensational photography, set design and other technical attributes"; Stephen Whitty (Newark Star-Ledger, 3.5/4) highlights "nightmarish visual imagery, an easy command of composition."
- **Pace & action:** Soren Andersen (Seattle Times, 4/4) calls the pace "delirious" and the stunts "incredible"; Chris Vognar (Dallas Morning News, A-) says the film keeps topping itself with "something even more outlandish and imaginative than what you just saw."
- **Performances:** Andersen praises Tom Hardy's "marvel of subdued conviction" and Charlize Theron's "impressive gravity" as Furiosa; Nathan notes the irony of Hardy being "the point of calm." Brian Tallerico (RogerEbert.com, 4/4) also commends the film for avoiding "paper-thin characters."
- **Filmmaking vision:** Michael O'Sullivan (Washington Post, 3/4) credits "Miller's nitro-burning aesthetic vision," and Cary Darling (Fort Worth Star-Telegram, 4/5) calls it a "surreal, operatic take on the action movie" that makes the earlier films "seem almost timid by comparison."

The main caveat, per Whitty, is that story flaws — "easy political posturing, too many shallow characters" — are outweighed by Miller's directorial strengths.

questions.question: What did critics dislike about Suicide Squad?
questions.answer:
**Suicide Squad (2016)** drew a fairly consistent set of complaints from critics:

- **Peter Travers (Rolling Stone)** argued director David Ayer compromised his "hardcore action bona fides" for a tame PG-13 crowd-pleaser "that would rather ingratiate than cut deep, or even cut at all."
- **Cary Darling (Fort Worth Star-Telegram/DFW.com)** called it loud rather than visionary — "volume is not vision" — and said it "turns out to be just another generic superhero action movie," despite some entertaining performances.
- **Marjorie Baumgarten (Austin Chronicle)** criticized the film for having "no one to root for," plot points that "lack coherence," and flashbacks that make it feel "fused into shape in the editing room."
- **Wendy Ide (Observer (UK))** said the film lacks "a credible antagonist," calling that "one of the many problems with Suicide Squad."
- **Michael O'Sullivan (Washington Post)** said the film aimed at but fell short of the teenage demographic, calling it "a double cop-out" that disappoints both fans of the source material's darker aesthetic and "discerning adolescents."
- **Roxana Hadadi (Chesapeake Family Magazine)**, while praising the visuals and the performances of Will Smith and Margot Robbie, concluded that "overall Suicide Squad is a sloppy mess."

Not every review was negative: **Tony Hicks (San Jose Mercury News)** gave it a fresh 2.5/4, describing it as a "semi-delightful mess" and a "sloppy and wild ride" worth enjoying for now.

For reference, the database lists the film at an IMDb rating of **5.9/10** (753,507 votes), directed by David Ayer.

It covers all major criticisms: the PG-13 compromise, generic nature, lack of coherent plot, absence of a credible antagonist, tonal mismatch with source material, and the 'sloppy mess' characterization. questions.question: What do critics say about Heath Ledger's performance in The Dark Knight?
questions.answer:
Critics across the board praise Heath Ledger's Joker performance in *The Dark Knight* (2008):

- **Owen Gleiberman (Entertainment Weekly, A-)**: Ledger delivers "a maniacal gusto inspired enough to suggest that he might have lived to be as audacious an actor as Marlon Brando, and maybe as great" — noting it was the last performance he completed before his death.
- **Michael Phillips (Chicago Tribune, 4/4)**: "Ledger's work is improbably droll, impossibly creepy, meticulously detailed," and the standout among the film's "two-faced masquerading freaks."
- **Peter Howell (Toronto Star, 4/4)**: The film deserves consideration for Best Picture and Director "along with the expected Oscar kudos for Ledger."

Later critics in the database treat that performance as the benchmark: in *The Dark Knight Rises* (2012), Dann Gire (Chicago Daily Herald, 3/4) writes that "no villain could come close to matching Ledger's inspired Joker," and Robert Roten (Laramie Movie Scope, B) calls the sequel "a bit of a letdown, containing nothing close to the brilliance of the late Heath Ledger's performance in the previous film."

questions.question: What do critics say about Joaquin Phoenix in Joker?
questions.answer:
Critics consistently single out Joaquin Phoenix's performance as the driving force of *Joker* (2019), though they differ on how they characterize it:

- **Peter Travers (Rolling Stone, 4.5/5)** calls it "a gut-punch performance by Phoenix that puts a horrifically human face on an iconic comic-book villain," and dismisses the surrounding controversy.
- **Mark Daniell (Toronto Sun, 4/4)** credits Phillips and Phoenix together for "reimagining what a comic book movie can be" — one free of multi-movie setup that "can go to places other films in this genre can't."
- **Richard Roeper (Chicago Sun-Times, 3.5/4)** says Phoenix appears in virtually every minute and "dominat[es] the screen with his memorably creepy turn," leaving the film clinging "to you like the aftermath of an unfortunately realistic nightmare."
- **Donald Clarke (Irish Times, 4/5)** says Phoenix "kicks everything else into distant wings" and "spares no effort in keeping us diverted" on what he calls a "grim fairground ride."
- **Dwight Brown (National Newspaper Publishers Association, 2.5/4)** describes Phoenix as creating "a snake of a man with few to no redeeming qualities" in "a blistering performance that should get him a front row seat on Oscar night."
- **Matthew Lickona (San Diego Reader, 2/5)** is the outlier: while still marking the review fresh, he argues Phoenix "exemplif[ies] performing [rather than] acting," "creepily contorting as the Clown Prince of Crime" in Phillips' "timely, toxic take on the Making of a Murdering Madman."

In short, the reviews agree Phoenix dominates the film, but divide on whether that constitutes great acting or mere physical contortion.

questions.question: What do reviewers think of the visuals in Avatar?
questions.answer:
Reviewers widely praise *Avatar*'s visuals, though some question whether they change cinema:

**Positive:**
- **Ty Burr (Boston Globe)**, 3.5/4: "an entertainment to be not just seen but absorbed on a molecular level… Cameron aims for sheer wonderment, and he delivers."
- **Anne Thompson (indieWire)**, A: "a joyous celebration of story craft and the visual possibilities of cinema… Avatar is stunning," crediting Cameron and Weta Digital's technology.
- **Michael Phillips (Chicago Tribune)**, 3/4: Cameron "delivered the screen's most anticipated and persuasive blend of live-action and motion-capture animation to date."
- **Peter Bradshaw (Guardian)**, 3/5: "The effects of Avatar are certainly something to see, especially on an Imax screen the size of an upended football field" — though he adds "it's difficult to tell if the game has really been changed or not."

**Mixed/reserved:**
- **Tom Maurstad (Dallas Morning News)**, 3/5: "It is cool. But all this 'change the way you look at films' hype is just that… it looks like a video game."
- **Jake Coyle (Associated Press)**, 2.5/4: the effects are "clearly revolutionary," but the film "nevertheless feels unsatisfying and somehow lacks the pulse of a truly alive film."
- **Paul Byrnes (Sydney Morning Herald)**, 3/5: calls it "a beautiful folly, a technical wonder that represents a failure of nerve."

In short: the visuals themselves are nearly universally admired as groundbreaking and immersive, while the divide is over whether the spectacle translates into a satisfying film.

questions.question: What are the main criticisms of Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice?
questions.answer:
The critics in this dataset consistently raise several criticisms of *Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice*:

- **Lumbering and joyless tone**: Joshua Rothkopf (Time Out, 2/5) calls it "a lumbering, dead-on-arrival superhero mélange," and Ann Hornaday (Washington Post, 1.5/4) says that rather than "escapism and sensory exhilaration," viewers get heroes who "grimace, scowl and wince their way through heroics with the joyless determination of shift workers making the doughnuts."
- **Derivative, unoriginal storytelling**: Stephen Whitty (Newark Star-Ledger, 2/4) describes the film as a "greatest-hits medley of every superhero movie ever made — a little Dark Knight Rises here, a bit of Batman Begins there," adding that "none of it convinces."
- **Incoherent narrative**: Preston Jones (Fort Worth Star-Telegram, 1/5) argues that the film sacrifices "logic, reason and character motivation," likening it to "Hollywood's latest exercise in fan service" with screenplay ingredients thrown "in a blender and filming the scraps."
- **A disappointment for the genre**: Rothkopf frames it as "a $250 million tombstone for a genre in dire need of a break."

Overall, the database's critic average for the film is 4.9/10 (from 20 rated reviews in the database), with most scores clustered in the middle-lower range (no review above 8, and several in the 2–4 band). Note these review excerpts are all negative; the distribution indicates some more positive reviews exist in the data but are not shown here.

questions.question: Do critics think Gravity is worth seeing?
questions.answer:
Yes — the critics in this database are uniformly positive about *Gravity* (2013), with all six reviews listed as "fresh":

- **Ann Hornaday (Washington Post), 4/4** — says it "must be seen in theaters to be appreciated," arguing that watching it on anything less than a 40-foot screen is "tantamount to listening to Beethoven through a tin can and a string."
- **Christy Lemire (ChristyLemire.com), 4/4** — "Believe the hype: Gravity is as jaw-droppingly spectacular as you've heard," praising it as magnificent technically but also "a marvel of controlled acting and precise tone."
- **Matt Zoller Seitz (RogerEbert.com), 4/4** — highlights that, in its heart, "it is not primarily a film about astronauts, or space, or even a specific catastrophe."
- **Lou Lumenick (New York Post), 4/4** — calls it "a visually enthralling popcorn movie" that "will rivet vast crowds" over its running time "with not a second wasted."
- **Mark Kermode (Observer (UK)), 4/5** — praises its "level of sheer visual invention that would have left Stanley Kubrick's head spinning."
- **A.A. Dowd (AV Club), B+, fresh** — says the film "makes the case for throwing immense resources at true visionaries," with Cuarón "expertly" blending "the epic with the intimate."

In short, the available reviews consistently present it as worth seeing — several specifically urging the theatrical experience for its scale and visual craft.

questions.question: What do critics say about the music in La La Land?
questions.answer:
Critics' comments on *La La Land*'s music focus less on specific songs and more on how the film uses the musical form:

- **Mick LaSalle** (San Francisco Chronicle, 4/4) notes the "impersonal splashiness of the opening number" but says the film becomes "a film of great intimacy."
- **Joe Dziemianowicz** (New York Daily News, 5/5) says the movie "understands and celebrates what makes musicals tick. People sing because they feel so much. Emotions have to come out."
- **Mara Reinstein** (Us Weekly, 4/4) calls it "a gorgeous homage to the golden age of Hollywood musicals in the 1950s."
- **Ian Freer** (Empire, 5/5) describes it as "audacious, retro, funny and heartfelt" — "the latest great musical for people who don't like musicals."
- **Peter Rainer** (Christian Science Monitor, A) singles out the finale, which ends with a "what-might-have-been fantasia" and "a bluesy jazz piano chord, full of hurt and healing, that slowly fades to silence."
- **Stephen Whitty** (Newark Star-Ledger, 3.5/4) frames the music as serving the fantasy: "There's a genre which isn't afraid to recreate what romance actually feels like. And that's where 'La La Land' soars."
- **Candice Frederick** (Reel Talk Online, B-), the most reserved, calls the film "fun and cutesy" but implies it falls short of a truly great movie musical.

The available excerpts don't include detailed critiques of individual songs or the score itself — no reviewer breaks down the compositions or performances beyond the broader points above.

questions.question: Which film follows journalists uncovering child abuse covered up by the Catholic Church in Boston?
questions.answer:
**Spotlight** (2015).

The database overview states: "The true story of how the Boston Globe uncovered the massive scandal of child molestation and cover-up within the local Catholic Archdiocese, shaking the entire Catholic Church to its core."

- **David Stratton** (The Australian): "Spotlight is a celebration of the freedom of the press, a riveting story of investigative journalism and of the role played by The Boston Globe in bringing to public attention the terrible crimes that had been taking place in the city for decades."
- **Steven D. Greydanus** (National Catholic Register): the film "plunges us into the rhythms of a specific time and place: Boston around the turn of the millennium."
- **Lou Lumenick** (New York Post) on how "journalists can get co-opted by the institutions they cover" and "how much courage it takes to pursue a story that may alienate many of your readers."

The film is directed by Tom McCarthy and stars Mark Ruffalo, Michael Keaton, and Rachel McAdams; it holds an IMDb rating of 8.1.

questions.question: Which movie is about a young woman and her son held captive in a small shed for years?
questions.answer:
That description matches **Room (2015)**, directed by Lenny Abrahamson and written by Emma Donoghue.

- Per the film's overview: "Held captive for 7 years in an enclosed space, a woman and her young son finally gain their freedom, allowing the boy to experience the outside world for the first time."
- Philippa Hawker (The Age) calls it "a powerful imagining of an extraordinary situation" as well as "a poignant evocation of the ordinary, everyday intensity and complexity of the bond between mother and child."
- David Jenkins (Little White Lies) describes it as "a moving feminist tract which explores questions of what it means to be a mother, what it means to give love, and what it means to receive it."
- Amy Nicholson (L.A. Weekly) notes Abrahamson's fascination with "how Jack can see joy in this dungeon, and how Joy can dream of freedom when her son can't comprehend that there's anywhere else to go."

The film stars Brie Larson and Jacob Tremblay, runs 118 minutes, and holds an IMDb rating of 8.1. Note that the sources describe the setting as an enclosed space/"dungeon" rather than specifically a "small shed."
